hints: Focus on telophase: the sister chromatids have already separated, so how many chromosomes are now in just one of the two new nuclei?
Remember each single chromatid chromosome has two ends, so how many telomeres does one chromosome contribute? Multiply that by the number in one nucleus.
walkthrough:
**Count chromosomes in one telophase nucleus**

Think of mitosis as sharing out an identical set to each end of the cell. The parent cell has 38 chromosomes, so after anaphase each new nucleus gets a full set of 38.

We only count one nucleus, not both together.

**Recall what a telomere is**

A telomere is the protective cap at the end of a chromatid. A chromosome made of one chromatid has two ends, top and bottom, so it has 2 telomeres.

**Apply this to telophase**

In telophase the chromosomes are single chromatid chromosomes because the sister chromatids separated in anaphase. So each of the 38 chromosomes contributes 2 telomeres.

Key calculation:
$$38 \text{ chromosomes} \times 2 \text{ telomeres per chromosome} = 76 \text{ telomeres}$$

options.A: This counts only one telomere per chromosome. Every chromosome has two ends, so you need to double the chromosome number.
options.B: One nucleus has 38 single-chromatid chromosomes, each with 2 telomeres, giving 38 x 2 = 76. Well done!
options.C: 114 has no biological basis here. It would be 38 x 3, but chromosomes do not have three ends.
options.D: 152 would be correct before anaphase when each chromosome still has two chromatids (38 x 4). In telophase the chromatids have separated, so halve this.
